translations.text: The Life of our holy and blessed father John, abbot of Sinai, renowned for his teaching, enlightener of souls and truly blessed, which was written down by Daniel, a monk of Raithu.
Beloved brothers, my speech is not able to say what city it was in which this valiant soldier of the service of God was born and raised,

…before his first entry into the arena of ascetic struggle, for I do not know this for certain. But as for which city it is in which he now dwells and delights in the blessedness of immortality, that all-praised one,

I am not at all ignorant of that city. For he now dwells in the city whose inhabitants are those of whom Paul, the loud-sounding trumpet of the Church, preaches that their citizenship is in heaven. There this blessed one dwells, and he delights openly in those good things of which one never has enough.

With his mind he contemplates that invisible and incomprehensible goodness, and the rewards his sweat deserved are poured out upon him. For his labours he has received the kingdom of heaven as his honour, and he is, and will be forever, with those with whom…
feet stand in uprightness.
But how this material being was joined with those immaterial ones, I will relate to you well.

The blessed one was sixteen years old in bodily age, but a thousand years old in the wisdom of his mind, when he offered himself in this way as a sacrifice, a willing offering, to that great High Priest,
to whom he offered his body on Mount Sinai and his soul on the mountain of heaven.

And so, through that voluntary exile which is the leader of the virtues, he uprooted the passion of boldness down to its root, and acquired beautiful humility, and thoroughly drove away that deceiving passion of being a law to oneself and following one's own will;
for he bowed his neck to a spiritual teacher, so that he might travel without toil and without being tossed by waves on that harsh sea of this life.
And thus he subjected himself to his teacher as though he had a soul without speech and separated from will.
And this was wondrous: that he who was educated in the wisdom of philosophy became the disciple of a man who was simple in bodily learning.

But by heavenly understanding and humility he drove away the arrogance of philosophy. And the name of his teacher, who tonsured him, was Martyrius, who was settled in the innermost desert of holy father Anthony, which is near the Red Sea. Then pagans who live in those mountains fell upon their monastery, and they laid waste the monasteries and killed six of the fathers; and one of those killed was named Conon, and he was a knower of hidden things, and the grace of prophecy was with him.

But Father Martyrius took up their bodies and buried them in a cave, and he blocked the door of that cave with very large stones, and plastered it with lime, and wrote on it the names of those saints.

And after two days he went to look at their tomb, lest perhaps one of the beasts had dug something up, and he found the inscription on it untouched, and the sign that had been placed on the tomb as a marker unchanged. Then he opened it and went inside to take them out, and when he had gone in he did not find two of their bodies, for by the command of God they had been translated to wherever he willed: the body of Abba Conon and the body of another great brother. But let us return to our earlier account. For when our blessed father John became a monk he was sixteen years old, and Abba Martyrius took him to John, that blessed elder who had settled in the outer desert of Kedar, and with him was his disciple Stephen. And when the elder saw them, he rose and poured water into a small basin, and he washed the feet of the disciple and kissed his hands, but he did not wash the feet of his teacher. And Stephen, the elder's disciple, was scandalized in his heart when he saw this.

And when Abba Martyrius and his disciple had gone away, the elder, Father John, knew, for he was a knower of hidden things, that the disciple was scandalized in his heart. And the elder said to him: "Why are you scandalized, my son? Truly I tell you that I do not know this boy except as abbot of Mount Sinai, and it is the feet of the abbot that I have washed." And after forty-three years that boy became abbot on Mount Sinai, as the elder had prophesied about him. And not only did this elder alone prophesy about him,
but also Eustratius the solitary, who never came outside from the day on which Father Anastasius, abbot of Sinai, blessed him as a monk.

He saw him coming down from the holy mountain with his teacher, and the elder called to Father Abba Martyrius and to the boy as well, and he said to the elder: "Tell me, father, who is this boy, and who is it that tonsured him?" Father Martyrius said to him: "He is your servant, father, and my disciple." The holy father Eustratius said to him: "Blessed are you, Father Martyrius! Let someone go and tell Father Anastasius, abbot of Sinai, that the abbot of Mount Sinai has been tonsured today." And truly, just as the holy fathers prophesied concerning our blessed father, the blessed John, so he was perfect and worthy of it, and in every way he was perfect in every kind of good virtue; for this reason the fathers of Mount Sinai called him a second Moses. And when this blessed man became eighteen years old, he sent his teacher and instructor ahead to the King of heaven as an intercessor and suppliant, while he himself went out to do battle in the desert, holding his prayers in his hands as weapons. And so he entered the struggle of solitude, about five miles away from the great monastery, and he built his dwelling in a place called Tholas, and there he spent forty years without any faintheartedness;
and with that fierce love of God he was continually inflamed, as if by fire.
But who could declare in words the struggles that he accomplished there,
Or who could recount his deeds, all of whose virtues were carried out hidden from people? For his food was such
that one cannot live without it, and even that was little. With great want he subdued that tyrannical
belly and put a bridle on it. By living in the desert and not seeing anyone's face, he completely quenched the flame of the furnace of the passions,
until he had turned it entirely to ash and dust.
And idolatry, which is the love of silver and gold, he bravely overcame through hope in God and the virtue of poverty.

He made the slackness of the soul disappear with the goad of the remembrance of death. And love of kin, and of other worldly things, he loosened and drove away by remembering those immaterial and eternal good things.
The tyranny of anger had already been slain by him long before with the sword of obedience. And by abundant stillness and silence he tore apart the nets of ostentation and arrogance.
Who could fittingly describe the measure of his humility,
or the height of his perfect purity, which obedience began as a Bezalel, but which the Lord of the heavenly Jerusalem completed by his coming,

without which the devil and his powers of many wiles are not overthrown? Where shall I place, in this crown we are weaving, the fountain of his tears, a thing found in few? His hidden chamber still exists today: a small cave in a rocky place, a short distance from his cell, just far enough that his voice could not be heard.

But it was close to the heavens by the loudness of the voice of his lamentations, and his prayer rose up to the hearing of God. His tears were more burning than those of people who are being cut with the sword, or burned with fire, or whose eyes someone is plucking out.

He took only as much sleep as would keep his mind from being harmed by too much wakefulness. Before sleeping he prayed a great deal, and he wrote books, for he had this as his handiwork and as a remedy against despondency.

His whole course was lofty prayer and boundless love for God. Night and day, through the purity of virginity, he beheld Him in the purified mirror of his own soul, and he never had enough of gazing on Him.

Moved by this, a brother named Moses became zealous and begged to become his disciple and servant, so that he might learn the true divine wisdom from him. He also got many people to plead with him on his behalf, so that he would grant his request.

Then that God-clothed man accepted him because he begged him to, and taught him every good thing. One day the blessed man ordered brother Moses to bring a little earth to make a vegetable bed. Moses went to the place he had been told and was carrying out his instruction.
When it was just about midday and the heat grew strong, Moses went in under a great rock and fell asleep.
But the Lord, who does not want any of his servants to suffer distress, hurried to help him;
for while the blessed John was praying in his cell,
he dropped off to sleep,
and he saw what seemed to be a certain man, a handsome priest, who was waking him, speaking to him and reproaching him for his sleep: "Ah, John, how carelessly you sleep!
"…but your disciple Moses is in danger." At once he woke up and prayed for his disciple.
In the evening, when Moses came back, the blessed man asked him, "Has some trouble come upon you, my son?"

And he said to him: "A great boulder was about to fall on me, father, for I was sleeping beneath it. But I heard your voice, as though you were calling me, and so I ran out of that place, and as soon as I had come out, that great boulder fell." But the humble-minded man did not tell him of that vision, but

secretly, with spiritual song, he sang praise and glorified the good God. And the blessed man was a model of goodness and a physician of spiritual wounds. For this reason there once came to the saint a certain monk named Isaac,
who was being overpowered by the battles of the flesh and had lost heart in fighting them. He came to that God-clothed man and confessed those battles to him, weeping and in tears.
The blessed man was amazed at his faith and said, "Let us both stand up to pray, beloved,"
And when they had finished the prayer and Isaac had bent his knees, God then fulfilled the will of the one who feared him, as David said.

And that serpent fled, driven out by the prayer, and the sick man saw himself healed, and he gave thanks to God, who glorifies those who glorify him, and bowed down before that blessed physician. But certain men, seized by envy,

called him a great talker and a boaster. These he instructed by deed, so as to convince them that he has power for all things through Christ who strengthens him: he fell silent from teaching for one year, although all used to come to him as to a physician and be enlightened. And he remained silent until those very accusers became his supplicants and said that a spring pouring forth benefits for the soul had been stopped up, and that the life of many was perishing.
So, after many people pressed him, he gave in again, and as before he taught and enlightened everyone. And so, when everyone saw how many his virtues were and how deep his teaching was. And after
his forty years of solitude, like a newly revealed Moses,
the monks of Sinai, using great pressure, made him abbot over the brothers. They lifted that shining lamp onto the lampstand of the abbacy. And those who call him a second Moses are not mistaken,
for he too went into the mountain, into the invisible cloud, and brought back the divinely written law, and by the word of God he opened his mouth and received the Spirit,
and he uttered a good word, or rather good words, from the good treasury of his heart.

And thus he completed that holy life of his as abbot of the true Israelites, who are the monks, and he passed to God, to the kingdom of heaven. And in one thing only he did not become like Moses: it did not befall him to be unable to enter the heavenly Jerusalem, as Moses was unable to enter the earthly Jerusalem; rather, he attained to that heavenly Jerusalem, together with that great Moses himself.
And many are witnesses of his virtues, who were saved and are being saved through those divine words of his, and who have seen him and know him.

A witness is Father David, set apart [?] in wisdom, to the life of that blessed man. A witness also is the blessed John, shepherd of us Raithenes, who entreated that God-clad man to write down for us the teachings of the monastic life. And that new seer of God came down to us in mind from Mount Sinai,
and he too showed us those divinely written tablets, on which were written, on the outside, the teachings of practice and, on the inside, the teachings of contemplation, to the glory of God.
To him be glory, now and always and forever and ever.
Amen.
